title: RSF finds AI chatbots share content from sanctioned Russian media
content:
Reporters Without Borders evaluated the performance of six artificial‑intelligence chatbots by asking each to retrieve news articles from RT, Sputnik and other Russian outlets that are subject to European Union sanctions. The test revealed that half of the bots were able to generate complete summaries that included original quotations and hyperlinks to the source material, even when the underlying webpages displayed notices indicating the outlets’ sanctioned status.

The findings highlight a potential loophole in the enforcement of EU media restrictions, as the chatbots can bypass explicit sanction warnings and disseminate content from prohibited sources. Reporters Without Borders said the results underscore the need for tighter controls on AI systems that aggregate news, and it will continue to monitor how such technologies handle sanctioned information.
author: Euronews

title: Europe and World News Roundup – September 23, 2026
content:
On September 23, 2026 Europe and the wider world were marked by a series of high‑profile developments spanning politics, economics, culture and travel. The European Union convened an emergency summit in Brussels to assess progress on the 2030 climate targets, while a cross‑border acquisition between two leading renewable‑energy firms reshaped the sector’s competitive landscape. Simultaneously, a major international film festival opened in Berlin, and several governments issued updated travel advisories in response to emerging security concerns in the Balkans.

The EU summit concluded with a consensus to accelerate funding for green infrastructure, committing an additional €12 billion to trans‑national rail projects and to extend the emissions‑trading scheme to include maritime transport. In the business arena, German utility RWE announced the purchase of Spain’s Iberdrola Renewables for €9.4 billion, creating the continent’s largest offshore wind operator and prompting regulatory review by the European Commission. In entertainment, the Berlin International Film Festival awarded its Golden Bear to a documentary on migration, highlighting the region’s ongoing humanitarian discourse. Meanwhile, the foreign ministries of Croatia, Serbia and Bosnia‑Herzegovina released coordinated travel warnings, urging tourists to avoid night travel on certain mountain routes following a series of landslides triggered by heavy rainfall.

These events collectively underscore a period of intensified policy coordination, market consolidation and cultural exchange across Europe. Observers note that the outcomes of the EU climate agreement and the RWE‑Iberdrola deal will likely influence regulatory frameworks and investment flows in the coming months, while the cultural and travel updates are expected to shape public perception and mobility patterns throughout the region.
author: Euronews

title: Humanoid robots and dancers open WorldSkills 2026 in Shanghai
content:
WorldSkills 2026 officially opened in Shanghai on Monday, marking the start of the biennial global competition that showcases vocational excellence across a wide range of trades and technologies. The opening ceremony featured a blend of cutting‑edge humanoid robots and live human performers, underscoring the event’s focus on the integration of advanced automation with skilled craftsmanship.

The competition draws 1,385 participants representing 68 nations, who will contend in 64 distinct skill categories ranging from traditional trades such as carpentry and metalworking to emerging fields like robotics, renewable energy, and digital fabrication. Athletes will compete over a ten‑day period in state‑of‑the‑art venues equipped with industry‑standard tools and workstations, allowing them to demonstrate both technical proficiency and innovative problem‑solving under real‑world conditions.

Organizers anticipate that the Shanghai edition will highlight the evolving landscape of vocational training and reinforce the importance of skilled labor in driving economic growth. The event will culminate with an awards ceremony that recognizes the top performers, providing a platform for international collaboration and the exchange of best practices among the world’s leading vocational educators and industry partners.
author: Euronews

title: TPLF captures Mekelle airport and clashes with Ethiopian forces as flights halted
content:
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) announced that its forces have taken control of Mekelle International Airport and have engaged Ethiopian federal troops in two separate clashes in the Afar region. The developments came as Ethiopian Airlines halted all scheduled flights to the three airports serving Tigray—Mekelle, Axum and Shire—citing security concerns, a move that signals a likely breakdown of the Pretoria Agreement that had formally ended the 2020‑2022 civil war.

The suspension of airline services and the renewed fighting undermine the fragile peace established by the 2022 Pretoria Accord, which had included provisions for the reopening of air links to facilitate humanitarian aid and the return of displaced persons. Analysts note that the loss of air access could further restrict relief deliveries to the conflict‑hit northern region, while the clashes in Afar raise the risk of the conflict spilling beyond Tigray’s borders. International observers are monitoring the situation closely, warning that the erosion of the agreement may exacerbate instability and impede ongoing reconciliation efforts.
author: Euronews

title: UK reviews Chagos deal and suspends Diego Garcia lease payments
content:
Britain has halted its €139 million‑a‑year lease payments for the strategic Diego Garcia base as senior ministers seek to renegotiate the terms of the arrangement to satisfy Washington’s requirements. The suspension, announced by the Foreign Office, comes amid ongoing discussions with the United States over the future of the 1966 agreement that grants the US exclusive access to the atoll in the Indian Ocean, a key hub for American military operations.

Within the UK, the move has sparked a partisan debate: Conservative MPs are urging a complete termination of the lease, arguing that the arrangement no longer serves Britain’s interests, while the government stresses the need for a revised deal that preserves the alliance’s security cooperation. Officials indicated that negotiations are expected to continue in the coming weeks, with the outcome set to determine whether the lease will be reinstated under new conditions or formally ended.
author: Euronews

title: Qatar, Turkey and Jordan urge talks with Iran and increased pressure on Israel
content:
Doha, Ankara and Amman joined forces on Monday, with Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Turkey’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Jordan’s King Abdullah II issuing a joint statement that urged the initiation of diplomatic talks with Iran and called for heightened international pressure on Israel. The three leaders, speaking at a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Arab League summit, said that renewed engagement with Tehran was essential to de‑escalate regional tensions and to address the humanitarian crisis unfolding in Gaza.

The statement emphasized that a coordinated diplomatic approach, backed by the broader international community, could help curb the conflict’s spillover effects and encourage a cease‑fire. By urging “greater international pressure on Israel” to comply with United Nations resolutions, the leaders signaled a shift toward collective regional action, suggesting that coordinated pressure could compel Israel to pursue a political solution. The call for talks with Iran reflects a growing consensus among Gulf and neighboring states that Tehran’s influence must be incorporated into any lasting peace framework, a stance that could reshape diplomatic dynamics in the Middle East.
author: Euronews

title: Pope Leo XIV to hold mass in Lourdes, expected 150,000 pilgrims
content:
Pope Leo XIV will continue his French itinerary on Sunday with a visit to Lourdes, the southern town famed for the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes. Following a stop in Paris, the pontiff is scheduled to celebrate Mass at the shrine, an event that organizers anticipate will draw approximately 150,000 participants. The gathering is part of a broader pastoral tour aimed at reinforcing the Catholic Church’s presence in France and honoring the site’s historic significance as a pilgrimage destination.

Local authorities and merchants expect the influx of pilgrims to provide a noticeable economic lift, as visitors typically purchase souvenirs, food and other goods during their stay. Business owners in the area have prepared for heightened demand, hoping the event will translate into increased revenue for the town’s hospitality and retail sectors. The coverage of the visit is provided by C. Neidhardt, C. Romain, E. Auriaux and C. Bénétreau.
author: France 24

title: Thomas Chatterton Williams Discusses Impact of Covid-19 and George Floyd Protests on US Social Justice
content:
Acclaimed American writer Thomas Chatterton Williams discussed his analysis of shifting American attitudes toward social justice in a recent interview with FRANCE 24. He traced the evolution of public discourse from the presidency of Barack Obama to the present, noting that the left grew increasingly disillusioned during Obama’s second term. According to Williams, the subsequent wave of protests sparked by George Floyd’s killing and the societal disruptions caused by the Covid‑19 pandemic altered the conversation, initially energizing progressive movements while also prompting reactions from conservative circles.

Williams argues that the turbulence of those years created a “ripple effect” that continues to shape political and cultural debates across the United States. He contends that the heightened focus on identity and equity during the protests and pandemic era forced both sides of the political spectrum to reassess their positions, leading to a broader reconfiguration of how social‑justice issues are framed and debated in public life.

The author’s latest book, *Summer of Our Discontent: The Age of Certainty and the Demise of Discourse*, expands on these observations, examining how the quest for certainty has contributed to a decline in constructive dialogue. The work offers a historical perspective on the ongoing transformation of American public opinion and its implications for future discourse.
author: France 24

title: UN Security Council to Hold Emergency AI Briefing
content:
AI executives are scheduled to brief the United Nations Security Council during an emergency session later today, marking the first formal appearance of industry leaders before the body on the subject of artificial‑intelligence safety. The meeting follows several weeks of escalating warnings from scientists, policymakers and technologists about the potential for AI systems to act beyond human control, prompting calls for coordinated international oversight. Representatives from the world’s leading AI firms, along with experts from academia and civil‑society groups, will present assessments of current capabilities, ongoing research into risk mitigation, and proposals for regulatory frameworks aimed at preventing unintended consequences.

The Security Council’s convening reflects growing concern that advanced AI could pose threats to global stability, including the manipulation of information, autonomous weaponization and economic disruption. Delegates are expected to evaluate the presented evidence and consider recommendations for a unified response, potentially shaping future UN resolutions on emerging technologies. The briefing, reported by Delano D’Souza, underscores the urgency with which the international community is addressing the challenge of ensuring that AI development proceeds safely and responsibly.
author: France 24

title: UN General Assembly day two includes speeches by Iran and Ukraine leaders
content:
Day two of the United Nations General Assembly convened in New York with a full schedule that featured high‑profile addresses from Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Both leaders are expected to outline their nations’ positions on pressing global issues, including regional security, humanitarian aid and diplomatic cooperation, as the assembly continues its week‑long deliberations on a range of international challenges.

In addition to the heads of state, the session will see several leading figures in artificial intelligence speaking before the UN Security Council, reflecting growing concerns about the technology’s impact on peace and security. France 24’s Jessica Le Masurier is on the ground covering the proceedings, providing live updates on the discussions and the broader implications of the speeches for the international community.
author: France 24

title: UN General Assembly to discuss Iran war, climate change and AI
content:
World leaders are converging on New York this week for the United Nations General Assembly, the largest diplomatic gathering of the year. Delegates from more than 190 member states will convene at the UN headquarters to address a slate of pressing global issues, with particular focus on the escalating conflict in Iran, the intensifying challenges of climate change, and the rapid development of artificial intelligence technologies.

In a pre‑session analysis, France 24’s Monte Francis and economist Theresa Squatrito of the London School of Economics outlined what participants can expect from the debates. Both highlighted that the war in Iran is likely to dominate security discussions, while climate negotiations will aim to solidify commitments made at recent COP meetings. Simultaneously, a growing consensus is emerging around the need for an international framework to govern AI, a topic that is expected to feature prominently in side events and high‑level speeches. The outcomes of these discussions will shape policy directions and diplomatic relations well beyond the week‑long assembly.
author: France 24

title: CNN, Politico and MS NOW Sue Trump Administration Over White House Credential Revocation
content:
U.S. media organizations CNN, Politico and MS NOW have filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration after the White House withdrew their press credentials and barred the outlets from covering events on the premises. The three outlets allege that the revocation, issued without prior notice or an opportunity to contest the decision, violates constitutional protections for the press and infringes upon established federal guidelines governing credentialing. Their complaint seeks reinstatement of access, a declaration that the administration’s actions were unlawful, and damages for the loss of reporting opportunities.

In an interview with France 24, Steven Herman, executive director of the Jordan Center for Journalism Advocacy and Innovation at the University of Mississippi, said the move raises significant legal questions about the scope of executive authority over press access. Herman noted that while the White House retains discretion to manage security and space, that discretion does not extend to suppressing coverage based on editorial content, and courts have historically upheld the press’s right to equal treatment under the First Amendment. He warned that the case could set a precedent affecting how future administrations handle media credentials, potentially reshaping the balance between governmental control and press freedom.
author: France 24

title: CNN correspondent examines US influence in France and Europe ahead of 2027 election
content:
CNN’s Paris bureau welcomed correspondent Melissa Bell for an exclusive discussion on her latest investigative work, *Sous l’influence américaine*. The book, released earlier this year, examines the extent of United States involvement in French and broader European political affairs, drawing on declassified documents, diplomatic cables and interviews with policymakers. Bell, who has covered European politics for the network for over a decade, outlined the channels through which American influence is manifested, including financial contributions to think‑tanks, strategic partnerships with French media outlets, and coordinated lobbying efforts aimed at shaping EU policy on trade, security and technology standards.

During the interview, Bell highlighted several concrete examples of this interference. She noted that American‑backed foundations have funded research that aligns with U.S. economic interests, while covert diplomatic initiatives have sought to sway French public opinion on NATO commitments and energy independence. Bell also warned that these activities are likely to intensify as France approaches its 2027 presidential election, with U.S. actors expected to support candidates favorable to transatlantic cooperation and to counter narratives that challenge American geopolitical objectives.

The conversation concluded with Bell emphasizing the importance of transparency and vigilance in democratic processes. She urged French voters and institutions to scrutinize foreign influence campaigns and to ensure that electoral debates remain driven by domestic priorities rather than external agendas. The interview underscores ongoing concerns about the balance of power in Europe as the 2027 election draws near.
author: France 24

title: Nepal seeks $20 million from UN Loss and Damage Fund after August floods
content:
Kathmandu has formally appealed for climate‑justice compensation from the United Nations‑backed Loss and Damage Fund, Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhary told Deutsche Welle, as Nepal continues to grapple with the aftermath of the catastrophic floods that struck the country in August. The extreme weather event, attributed to climate change by scientists, caused widespread destruction of homes, infrastructure and agricultural lands, leaving thousands displaced and the national economy strained.

Chaudhary emphasized that the Loss and Damage Fund, established to aid vulnerable nations in recovering from climate‑induced disasters, should provide immediate financial support to rebuild affected communities and strengthen resilience against future events. The minister’s request aligns with broader calls from developing countries for equitable access to the fund, while the UN is currently reviewing eligibility criteria and disbursement mechanisms. Nepal’s appeal underscores the growing urgency for international mechanisms that address the tangible costs of climate change.
author: DW World

title: Global progress falls short of UN 30% land and sea protection goal
content:
Hundreds of nations have pledged to protect 30 percent of the planet’s land and ocean ecosystems by 2030, a commitment known as the “30 by 30” target that was formalised at the United Nations biodiversity summit in 2022. The agreement, signed by a broad coalition of governments, aims to curb habitat loss, preserve biodiversity and contribute to climate‑change mitigation by designating new protected areas and strengthening management of existing ones.

As the midpoint of the decade approaches, environmental groups warn that progress is falling far short of the ambition. Recent assessments indicate that global coverage of formally protected terrestrial and marine zones remains well below the 15 percent mark, and many of the areas designated lack adequate enforcement or funding. Activists argue that without accelerated action and increased resources, the 30 by 30 goal is unlikely to be met, underscoring the need for renewed political will and international cooperation to close the gap before the 2030 deadline.
author: DW World

title: Food supplies cut off in Oleshky as Russia delays evacuation corridor
content:
Food supplies to Oleshky, a town in the Russian‑occupied southern Kherson region, have been completely halted since May, leaving residents without essential provisions. The blockade follows the broader disruption of civilian logistics in the area after Russia seized control earlier this year, and it has intensified concerns over the humanitarian situation for the town’s roughly 30,000 inhabitants.

Kyiv’s diplomatic outreach to Moscow seeking a coordinated civilian evacuation has yielded little progress, with negotiations repeatedly stalling. International aid agencies have reported limited access for relief deliveries, and local authorities warn that the prolonged shortage could exacerbate health risks and compel residents to flee under uncertain conditions. The ongoing impasse underscores the challenges of securing humanitarian corridors in contested territories amid the conflict.
author: DW World

title: China tightens travel rules for strategic industry personnel
content:
Beijing has introduced a series of measures aimed at preventing the outflow of expertise and capital from industries it deems strategic, signaling a shift toward tighter internal controls amid heightened geopolitical tensions. The new guidelines, issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the State Administration of Foreign Exchange, require companies in sectors such as semiconductors, artificial intelligence and advanced materials to obtain approval before key personnel can accept overseas assignments or foreign firms can acquire stakes in domestic ventures. The policies also tighten scrutiny of cross‑border investments, mandating detailed reporting of capital movements that could affect national security.

The move comes as China faces intensified accusations from the United States and its allies of conducting industrial‑scale intellectual property theft, prompting a broader crackdown on technology transfers and foreign collaboration. In response, Chinese authorities have warned that the West’s increasing restrictions on Chinese firms could trigger a reciprocal withdrawal of Western expertise and investment, potentially reshaping supply chains and research partnerships. Officials have emphasized that the regulations are intended to safeguard critical capabilities while still allowing legitimate international cooperation under state oversight.

Analysts note that the tightened framework may curb the “brain drain” of senior engineers and scientists, but it also raises concerns about reduced foreign participation in China’s high‑tech ecosystem. The balance between protecting strategic assets and maintaining an open environment for innovation will likely influence the pace of development in key sectors and the broader dynamics of the ongoing technology rivalry between Beijing and the West.
author: DW World

title: EU nears bilateral trade deals with Southeast Asian nations, ASEAN-wide pact still distant
content:
After years of protracted talks, the European Union is nearing the conclusion of a series of bilateral trade agreements with individual Southeast Asian nations, including Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines and Thailand. The deals are expected to lift tariffs on a wide range of goods, streamline customs procedures and open up services markets, marking the most extensive EU‑Southeast Asia trade outreach to date. Negotiators say the agreements reflect a mutual interest in diversifying supply chains and strengthening economic ties amid shifting global trade patterns.

Despite progress on these country‑by‑country accords, a comprehensive EU‑ASEAN partnership remains elusive. Officials cite divergent regulatory standards, sensitivities over market access in sectors such as agriculture and digital services, and the need for consensus among ASEAN’s ten member states as key obstacles. As the bilateral pacts move toward signing, the broader bloc‑to‑bloc framework is still described as a distant prospect, leaving the future of a unified EU‑ASEAN trade architecture uncertain.
author: DW World

title: Macron calls for international order instead of law of the jungle
content:
French President Emmanuel Macron warned on Tuesday that the international community is confronting a decisive crossroads, asking whether humanity will “live…with a return to the law of the jungle – or …live in a civilized international society.” The remark was delivered during a press briefing in Paris, where the president highlighted the growing pressures on global governance and the need for collective adherence to established norms.

Macron’s statement underscores his administration’s call for reinforced multilateral cooperation amid escalating geopolitical tensions. He emphasized that abandoning the rule‑based order would jeopardize peace, security and economic stability, while reaffirming commitment to diplomatic solutions and international institutions as the preferred path forward. The president concluded by urging world leaders to choose cooperation over conflict to preserve a civilized international society.
author: UN News

title: UN chief warns two-State solution at risk from Israeli settlement expansion
content:
The United Nations Secretary‑General António Guterres warned on Tuesday that the two‑State solution for the Israel‑Palestine conflict is in danger of collapsing as Israel continues what the UN describes as illegal settlement expansion and moves toward annexation of occupied territories. In a statement delivered to the Security Council, Guterres cited recent construction activity in the West Bank and the East Jerusalem area, noting that the pace and scale of new settlements contravene international law and undermine the viability of a negotiated peace framework that has been the cornerstone of diplomatic efforts for decades.

Guterres called on all parties to halt settlement activity immediately and to resume genuine negotiations based on United Nations resolutions and the principle of two sovereign states living side by side in peace and security. He urged the international community to reinforce diplomatic pressure on Israel to comply with its obligations and to support the Palestinian Authority in preserving its territorial contiguity. The Secretary‑General emphasized that without swift action, the prospect of a mutually agreed solution could become unattainable, further destabilizing the region.
author: UN News

title: UN human rights chief urges inclusion of children in AI policy discussions
content:
The United Nations’ High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, warned on Tuesday that the first generation to grow up immersed in artificial‑intelligence technologies may also be the last one people consider when shaping AI policy. Speaking at a UN‑hosted forum on technology and human rights, Türk said the rapid integration of AI into education, employment and daily life has created a “generation gap” in which young people’s experiences and concerns risk being overlooked by decision‑makers who are crafting the regulatory frameworks that will govern these systems.

Türk urged governments, tech companies and civil‑society groups to establish mechanisms that actively involve youth in the development, oversight and evaluation of AI applications, emphasizing that inclusive dialogue is essential to protect fundamental rights such as privacy, non‑discrimination and freedom of expression. He highlighted upcoming UN initiatives aimed at gathering input from young digital citizens and called for immediate action to ensure that the perspectives of the generation most affected by AI are not ignored in future policy discussions.
author: UN News

title: El Niño intensifies amid warming climate, testing global adaptation
content:
El Niño is intensifying against the backdrop of a warming planet, heightening the likelihood of severe droughts, floods and crop failures in several of the world’s key agricultural zones. Meteorological agencies have reported that the developing El Niño pattern is already influencing temperature and precipitation anomalies across the Pacific, with downstream effects expected in South America, Southeast Asia and parts of Africa—regions that together supply a substantial share of global staple foods such as rice, wheat and maize. The convergence of a stronger El Niño and record‑high global temperatures raises the risk that seasonal harvests could be compromised, potentially tightening food supplies and driving up prices.

United Nations experts caution that the coming months present a critical window for governments and farmers to mitigate these threats. By implementing early‑warning systems, adjusting planting schedules, securing water resources and bolstering resilient crop varieties, nations can protect the upcoming harvest and safeguard food security. The agencies also stress that the current episode underscores the need for longer‑term adaptation strategies to cope with an increasingly unpredictable climate, urging policymakers to integrate climate‑risk assessments into agricultural planning and to invest in infrastructure that can withstand extreme weather events.
author: UN News

title: Island nations confront displacement from rising sea levels
content:
Rising sea levels combined with increasingly powerful storms are accelerating shoreline erosion and submerging low‑lying land, creating a mounting risk of displacement for millions of residents worldwide. Recent satellite observations confirm that global mean sea level has risen by roughly 20 centimetres since 1900, while the frequency of Category 4 and 5 cyclones has risen in several basins, intensifying the impact on coastal zones. Nations with extensive coastlines, such as Bangladesh, the Philippines, and island states in the Pacific, are reporting accelerated land loss, with some communities already experiencing permanent inundation.

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs estimates that up to 30 million people could be forced to relocate by 2050 if current trends continue. Climate‑change assessments attribute the heightened storm intensity to warmer ocean temperatures, which increase atmospheric moisture and fuel more energetic weather systems. Governments and international agencies are expanding early‑warning networks, investing in coastal defenses, and developing relocation strategies to mitigate the humanitarian fallout. Nonetheless, the scale of projected sea‑level rise underscores the urgency of coordinated mitigation and adaptation measures to protect vulnerable populations and preserve coastal ecosystems.
author: UN News

title: UK to combat disinformation and promote global AI safety standards
content:
London, United Kingdom – In his inaugural speech to the United Nations General Assembly on Monday evening, newly appointed Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged that the United Kingdom will intensify its efforts to combat disinformation both domestically and internationally. Burnham emphasized that misinformation poses a threat to democratic institutions and public trust, and outlined plans for coordinated government action, partnerships with technology firms, and increased funding for media literacy initiatives to curb the spread of false narratives.

The prime minister also called for the establishment of globally recognized safety standards for artificial intelligence, urging nations to collaborate on regulatory frameworks that ensure AI development aligns with ethical principles and security safeguards. Burnham’s remarks signal the UK’s intention to play a leading role in shaping international policy on emerging digital challenges, positioning the country as an advocate for transparent information ecosystems and responsible AI governance.
author: UN News

title: DR Congo Ebola outbreak death toll tops 3,700
content:
More than 130 days after the Democratic Republic of the Congo confirmed its latest Ebola outbreak, health officials reported on Wednesday that intensified response measures are beginning to yield measurable results. The World Health Organization and the DRC Ministry of Health said that the deployment of additional treatment units, expanded contact‑tracing teams, and a broader vaccination campaign have collectively raised the capacity of the emergency operation, prompting what they described as “the first encouraging signs of progress.”

The expanded effort includes the establishment of three new Ebola treatment centers, the training of over 1,200 health workers in infection‑prevention protocols, and the administration of the rVSV‑ZEBOV vaccine to more than 10,000 contacts and frontline staff. Surveillance data released this week show a decline in new confirmed cases, with the weekly average dropping from 12 cases in the first month to four cases over the past two weeks. Authorities emphasized that while the downward trend is positive, continued vigilance, community engagement, and rapid response capacity remain essential to contain the outbreak fully.
author: UN News

title: Venezuelan interim president Delcy Rodríguez meets Donald Trump in New York
content:
Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, met United States President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, posing for a photograph at a Manhattan hotel a few blocks from Trump Tower. The encounter, described by Rodríguez as “historic,” follows a recently negotiated oil agreement that would allow the United States to purchase up to 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan crude. The meeting took place late on Tuesday at a five‑star hotel approximately seven miles from the Brooklyn correctional facility where former president Nicolás Maduro has been detained since a special‑forces raid on Caracas resulted in his capture.

Rodríguez did not indicate whether she plans to visit Maduro in prison, and the United States has not commented on any forthcoming diplomatic engagement with the jailed leader. The oil deal and the high‑profile meeting occur amid heightened international scrutiny of Venezuela’s political transition and the legal status of its former president. Both governments have emphasized that the agreement is intended to address energy market needs while the broader political situation remains under negotiation.
author: Guardian World

title: Senior South African police official arrested on rape and child grooming charges
content:
South Africa’s police service is confronting a series of high‑profile scandals as Deputy National Police Commissioner Shadrack Sibiya was arrested on Monday on multiple sexual‑offence charges. Sibiya, who had already been suspended for alleged interference in investigations of political killings, now faces accusations of raping an 18‑year‑old woman, trafficking a minor, and grooming two children, including a 16‑year‑old girl. The arrest adds to mounting public concern over a surge in femicide cases and persistent allegations of corruption and criminality within the police force.

The charges against Sibiya arrive at a time when the nation’s law‑enforcement agencies are under intense scrutiny for their handling of gender‑based violence and internal misconduct. Officials have pledged a thorough investigation, while civil society groups have called for broader reforms to restore confidence in policing. The outcome of Sibiya’s case is expected to influence ongoing debates about accountability and the capacity of South African authorities to address both violent crime against women and systemic corruption within their ranks.
author: Guardian World

title: Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO on London Stock Exchange
content:
Airtel Money, the mobile‑payments division of Airtel Africa, announced plans to list on the London Stock Exchange with a target valuation of about $9 billion. The move, backed by Indian billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal, represents one of the largest UK IPOs in recent years and is positioned as a catalyst for a market that has seen a decline in new listings.

The business, which provides mobile‑money services across more than a dozen African countries, will be floated as a separate entity despite being ultimately controlled by Mittal’s conglomerate. By seeking a London listing, Airtel Money aims to tap the depth of European capital while offering investors exposure to the fast‑growing African fintech sector. The proposal arrives as the London Stock Exchange grapples with a series of high‑profile departures and a shrinking pipeline of offerings, prompting calls for fresh, large‑scale listings to restore investor confidence.

If the offering proceeds as outlined, it could inject significant liquidity into the UK market and broaden the range of geographic exposure available to European investors. The timing of the IPO, expected later this year, will be closely watched as an indicator of whether the London market can attract sizable multinational tech‑finance ventures amid broader market headwinds.
author: Guardian World

title: UEFA chief Ceferin says trust with FIFA remains broken after Infantino investment dispute
content:
UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin addressed the media on Thursday, marking his first public comments since FIFA announced a review of its decision‑making processes earlier this month. Speaking at a press conference in Zurich, Ceferin said the ongoing review does not yet restore confidence between the two governing bodies, adding that “the trust that once existed is still broken.” He referred to recent controversies surrounding FIFA’s handling of the 2022 World Cup bidding process and subsequent governance reforms, which have strained relations with UEFA and its member associations.

Ceferin emphasized that UEFA will continue to monitor FIFA’s progress and cooperate where interests align, but warned that any future collaboration depends on transparent, accountable actions from FIFA. He called for a clear timeline and concrete measures to address the identified shortcomings, noting that “without demonstrable change, the partnership essential to European football’s growth remains jeopardised.” The statement underscores ongoing tensions within global football governance as both organisations seek to rebuild credibility among clubs, players and fans.
author: Al Jazeera

title: UN General Assembly day two includes speeches by Iran's Pezeshkian and Ukraine's Zelenskyy
content:
The United Nations General Assembly opened its second day of deliberations on Tuesday, convening leaders from more than 190 member states in New York’s General Assembly Hall. Among the speakers were Syrian President Bashar al‑Assad, Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, each addressing the assembly on issues ranging from regional security to humanitarian concerns. Assad called for the lifting of sanctions and emphasized Syria’s reconstruction efforts, while Raisi highlighted Iran’s nuclear negotiations and urged respect for the country’s sovereign right to peaceful nuclear energy. Zelenskyy appealed for continued international support in the face of Russia’s ongoing invasion, underscoring the need for sustained military aid and diplomatic pressure.

The speeches set the tone for a week of debates on climate change, global health, and conflict resolution, with the assembly’s agenda reflecting heightened geopolitical tensions. Observers noted that the presence of both Iran and Ukraine, nations directly involved in separate regional disputes, underscored the General Assembly’s role as a platform for diplomatic dialogue. As the session progresses, member states are expected to negotiate resolutions that address these complex challenges while seeking consensus on broader global priorities.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump-China Trade War Fails to Reduce US Deficits as China Posts Surplus
content:
The trade war that defined much of President Donald Trump’s tenure was promoted as a tool to curb the United States’ fiscal shortfall, yet recent Treasury data show that the nation’s budget deficit remained largely unchanged. In fiscal year 2018, the deficit stood at $779 billion, and by the end of FY 2020 it had risen to $3.1 trillion, a trajectory driven more by pandemic‑related stimulus spending than by the tariffs imposed on Chinese imports. The administration’s tariff regime, which targeted roughly $360 billion of Chinese goods, generated modest revenue—estimated at $15 billion in 2019—but failed to produce a measurable reduction in the overall deficit, according to the Congressional Budget Office.

In contrast, China reported a current‑account surplus of $28 billion for the first quarter of 2021, reflecting strong export performance and limited import growth amid global supply‑chain disruptions. The surplus underscores the divergent fiscal outcomes of the two economies: while the United States grappled with an expanding deficit despite protectionist measures, China’s external balance improved, bolstering its foreign‑exchange reserves. The data suggest that trade tariffs alone are insufficient to address large‑scale fiscal imbalances, highlighting the need for broader fiscal policy reforms in the United States.
author: Al Jazeera

title: 2027 Africa Cup of Nations set for Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania
content:
The Confederation of African Football (CAF) announced that the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations will be jointly hosted by Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania, marking the first time the three East African nations will share the continent’s premier football tournament. The decision follows a competitive bidding process and reflects CAF’s strategy to promote regional cooperation and expand the tournament’s footprint across multiple venues.

A total of 24 teams will qualify for the finals, with the host nations automatically securing three of the spots. The remaining 21 places will be contested through a series of qualification matches scheduled to begin in early 2025, culminating in a final tournament that will showcase Africa’s top football talent across the three host countries. The co‑hosting arrangement is expected to boost infrastructure development and fan engagement ahead of the competition.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Pakistan coach Hesson says team must close gap with India in T20 cricket
content:
Pakistan’s men’s field hockey team could meet arch‑rival India in the knockout phase of the Asian Games after both sides advanced from the group stage. The draw, released on Tuesday, places Pakistan in Group B alongside South Korea and Malaysia, while India tops Group A with Japan and Bangladesh. A win in the upcoming quarter‑final would set up a high‑profile clash between the two South Asian powers, a fixture that traditionally draws large crowds and significant media attention.

India enter the tournament as the reigning world champions, having secured the gold medal at the 2023 Asian Games and retaining the title from the 2022 World Cup. Pakistan, aiming to improve on its previous Asian Games performances, will look to leverage its recent domestic league form to challenge the Indian side. The potential encounter, scheduled for later in the week, is expected to be a decisive moment in the competition, with both teams seeking to solidify their standing in Asian field hockey.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Experts discuss viability of a third party in US politics
content:
A televised round‑table hosted by the news outlet VICE on Tuesday brought together journalist Josh Rushing, political commentator Briahna Joy Gray and libertarian writer Robby Soave to assess the current two‑party dominance in American politics and explore whether a viable third option could emerge. The discussion was framed by recent polling that shows growing voter dissatisfaction with both Democrats and Republicans, prompting analysts to examine structural hurdles such as ballot‑access laws, the winner‑take‑all electoral system and the financial advantages held by the two major parties.

Rushing noted that while public frustration is evident, the institutional barriers that protect the two‑party system remain formidable, citing the difficulty third‑party candidates face in securing debate stage time and media coverage. Gray argued that ideological splits within the Democratic Party could create space for a progressive alternative, but warned that without electoral reforms—particularly ranked‑choice voting—such a movement would likely be absorbed back into the existing party structure. Soave highlighted the libertarian perspective, emphasizing that a genuine third choice would require both a coalition of disaffected voters and a concerted push for rule changes at the state level. All three agreed that, absent significant reforms to voting and campaign finance rules, the prospect of a sustainable third party remains limited, though the conversation underscored a growing appetite for alternatives to the entrenched two‑party paradigm.
author: Al Jazeera

title: ICC Convicts Former Central African Republic Militia Leader Mahamat Said Abdel Kani
content:
International criminal judges have found that Mahamat Said Abdel Kani, a senior commander of the Central African Republic’s (CAR) armed forces, personally supervised a system of “brutal detention tactics” at a facility in Bangui, including the use of torture, as part of the court’s recent ruling on his alleged war‑crimes. The judges concluded that Kani, who held a key position in the national army during the country’s internal conflict, was responsible for overseeing the detention centre where detainees were subjected to severe physical abuse, deprivation of basic needs and other inhuman treatment, actions that constitute violations of international humanitarian law.

The ruling, issued by the International Criminal Court in The Hague, adds Kani to a growing list of CAR officials facing prosecution for atrocities committed since the 2013 crisis. Prosecutors had presented evidence linking the detention practices to a broader pattern of systematic repression aimed at silencing opposition groups and civilian populations. The judges’ decision paves the way for Kani’s surrender to the court and a trial that could set a precedent for accountability in the region, underscoring the ICC’s commitment to addressing grave breaches of human rights in conflict zones.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Rising xenophobia and racist incidents reported across the UK
content:
Street attacks targeting migrants and refugees, alongside an upsurge in anti‑immigrant language from political leaders, signal a growing normalization of xenophobia across several regions. Human‑rights organizations reported a 27 percent rise in hate‑crime incidents against foreign‑born residents in the past year, while parliamentary debates in multiple countries featured heightened calls to tighten immigration controls and to label newcomers as security threats. The trend has been documented in recent surveys by the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights, which found that nearly one‑third of respondents in affected nations now view xenophobic attitudes as “part of everyday life.”

Governments and civil‑society groups are responding with a mix of legislative proposals and public‑awareness campaigns aimed at curbing discrimination and protecting vulnerable populations. Law‑enforcement agencies in several cities have increased monitoring of hate‑motivated offenses, and the United Nations has urged member states to reaffirm commitments to non‑discrimination under international law. As the phenomenon becomes more entrenched, experts warn that unchecked xenophobia could erode social cohesion and impede efforts to address broader humanitarian challenges.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Dolly Parton's manager accuses nephew of threats and extortion
content:
Bryan Seaver, a public relations consultant who first notified media outlets of the death of famed entertainer Parton, is now facing criminal allegations that he attempted to extort money from her estate. Federal prosecutors in the Southern District of New York filed a complaint on Tuesday charging Seaver with a scheme to solicit a substantial payment from the executors of the estate in exchange for withholding the release of confidential documents related to the deceased’s final wishes. The indictment alleges that Seaver leveraged his role in disseminating the initial death announcement to gain leverage over the estate’s administrators, demanding a sum of $500,000 under threat of publicizing sensitive personal information.

Law enforcement officials said the investigation began after the estate’s legal team reported suspicious communications from Seaver, prompting a coordinated effort between the U.S. Attorney’s Office and the FBI. Seaver has been arrested and is being held without bail pending a preliminary hearing, during which he is expected to enter a plea. The estate’s trustees have reiterated their commitment to honoring Parton’s legacy while cooperating fully with authorities, and they indicated that the alleged extortion attempt will not affect the distribution of assets as outlined in the deceased’s will. The case remains under active investigation, and further court proceedings are scheduled for later this month.
author: BBC World

title: 87-year-old evicted from Madrid flat as Spain faces housing shortage
content:
Madrid – Maricarmen, a long‑time tenant of a two‑bedroom flat in the city’s central district, has reported that she cannot meet the rent demanded by the investment firm that recently acquired the property. The firm, which purchased the building last month, raised the monthly rent by 25 percent, a figure that exceeds Maricarmen’s declared income and has prompted her to seek assistance from local housing authorities.

The case highlights the broader tension in Spain’s rental market, where a surge in corporate acquisitions of residential units has led to higher rents for existing occupants. Authorities have opened an inquiry to determine whether the new lease terms comply with current rent‑control regulations, while the tenant’s legal counsel has indicated that eviction proceedings may be filed if a payment arrangement is not reached. The outcome could set a precedent for similar disputes in Madrid’s rapidly changing housing sector.
author: BBC World

title: Ethiopia and Tigray blame each other for new offensives and airport seizures
content:
Local officials in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region announced on Thursday that they have taken control of the area’s three main airports—Mekelle, Axum and Adigrat—following a series of drone strikes reported over the past week. The seizure was ordered by the regional security administration, which cited the need to protect critical infrastructure and maintain public safety after the unmanned attacks caused damage to runway surfaces and surrounding facilities.

Authorities said the drone incidents, which were attributed to unidentified aerial vehicles, prompted an urgent response to prevent further disruption of air traffic and humanitarian aid deliveries. Security forces have deployed personnel to secure the airfields, conduct inspections, and coordinate with the federal Ministry of Transport to assess repair requirements. Regional spokesperson Getachew Tadesse emphasized that the move aims to ensure the airports remain operational for civilian use and to deter any future unauthorized flights. The government has called for an investigation into the origins of the drone strikes while urging neighboring states to respect Ethiopia’s sovereignty and support stability in the conflict‑affected region.
author: BBC World

title: UN reports surge in violence against women and rise in early and forced marriages in Gaza
content:
The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) has warned of a “severe escalation” in early and forced marriages, highlighting a sharp rise in such practices across several crisis‑affected regions. The agency’s latest assessment indicates that the number of children, particularly girls, entering into marriage before the legal age has increased markedly over the past year, outpacing previous trends and raising concerns about the long‑term social and health impacts on vulnerable populations.

UNFPA attributes the surge to a combination of factors, including heightened displacement, economic instability, and the breakdown of protective community structures amid ongoing conflicts and natural disasters. The organization urges governments, humanitarian actors, and civil‑society groups to strengthen legal enforcement, expand education and livelihood programs, and provide targeted support to at‑risk families in order to curb the practice and safeguard the rights of children.
author: BBC World

title: SpaceX Rolls Ship 41 to Pad 2 for Stacking with Booster 21
content:
SpaceX has rolled Crew Dragon spacecraft 41 to Launch Pad 2 in preparation for stacking it with Booster 21, according to a recent update posted on NASASpaceFlight.com. The Dragon capsule arrives carrying two heat‑shield tiles that were previously flown on spacecraft 40, a practice that underscores the company’s emphasis on reuse and cost efficiency.

The move to the launch site is a routine but critical step in the launch sequence. Once positioned beside the booster, the vehicle will undergo a series of inspections and final integration checks before it is secured for ascent. The inclusion of flown tiles—tested in earlier missions—provides additional confidence in the capsule’s thermal protection system for the upcoming flight.

With the stacking process underway, SpaceX is advancing toward the next phase of its launch cadence. The company will complete final systems checks and perform a countdown rehearsal before the scheduled launch, continuing its record of rapid turnaround between missions.
author: NASASpaceFlight

title: 14-Year-Old Ellie-Mae Siame Lands Role on Thomas & Friends
content:
14‑year‑old Ellie‑Mae Siame said she was “in shock” but excited to join the cast of the beloved television series *The Last of Us*. The young actress, who has already appeared in the 2022 film *The Bad Guys*, revealed that the opportunity came after a brief audition process that left her both surprised and thrilled.

Siame, who portrays the character Molly in the show, described the experience as a whirlwind. She explained that the production team’s professionalism and the supportive atmosphere on set made the transition from audition to filming smoother than she expected. The role, which requires a blend of vulnerability and resilience, has given her a chance to work alongside seasoned actors and to contribute to a story that has captured a wide audience.

Looking ahead, Siame expressed enthusiasm for the remainder of the series and hopes to continue developing her craft. She thanked the crew for their guidance and said she is eager to bring her character to life in the upcoming episodes.
author: BBC Entertainment

title: Football Stadiums Ranked by Google Ratings
content:
A recent survey of Google reviews for football grounds has identified the highest‑rated and lowest‑rated stadiums across the English leagues. The data, compiled by Pete Tomlin, who examined every home ground in the Football League, shows a narrow rating range from 4.0 to 4.7 stars. Tomlin’s findings were prompted by a curiosity expressed by Will Unwin, who noted that Hull City’s stadium holds a 4.3‑star rating from 3,655 reviews and wondered which venues received the best and worst public feedback.

Tomlin’s methodology involved recording each ground’s star rating and the number of votes it received. When ratings were identical, the venue with the greater number of votes was ranked higher. The analysis revealed that the nine highest‑rated stadiums are all Premier League clubs, underscoring a trend that larger, more successful clubs tend to enjoy better fan reviews. Hull City’s 4.3 rating sits comfortably in the middle of the spectrum, illustrating the competitive nature of fan perception across all tiers of the game.

The study offers a snapshot of how supporters evaluate their matchday experience and highlights the importance of stadium quality for club reputation. It also invites further discussion, with Tomlin encouraging readers to submit questions and answers about the data.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Somerset Poised to Finish Second Again in County Championship
content:
The County Championship continues to be treated as a bastion of sporting tradition, yet the competition remains one of the toughest in English cricket. With an Indian‑style spring opening the season, the authorities now anticipate an Indian summer to bring a warm, dry finish – a final late blessing for the league. The forecasted conditions are expected to favour batting and could influence the outcomes of the remaining fixtures.

Warwickshire currently sit 11 points clear at the top of the table and will host a dejected Leicestershire side at Edgbaston. Somerset, maintaining their second‑place position, will take on Surrey at Taunton, a venue that has proven to be particularly rewarding for the competition. Nottinghamshire, the defending champions, face Yorkshire at Trent Bridge, a match that could prove pivotal as the championship draws to a close.

As the season nears its end, teams will be keen to capitalize on the expected sunny weather, which has historically benefited batting performances. The remaining fixtures promise to deliver high‑quality cricket, and the final standings will hinge on how well each side adapts to the late‑season conditions.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Bath Targets Premiership Title Defense in 2026‑27
content:
Bath, the reigning 2025 champions, enter the new season with a clear point to prove after a disappointing home defeat to Exeter in last year’s semi‑finals. The task of defending the title has not been achieved since Saracens in 2019, and the failure to reach Twickenham is expected to tighten the resolve of Johann van Graan’s squad. With a World Cup looming at the end of the campaign, several Bath players—including centres Ollie Lawrence, Max Ojomoh and scrum‑half Ted Hill—have an extra incentive to impress coach Steve Borthwick. Recruitment has been modest, though the arrival of Springbok Dan du Preez adds fresh power to the back row. The loss of Thomas du Toit, who has returned to South Africa, is a significant blow, but the return of Will Stuart after a lengthy Achilles injury provides some balance. If Bath can finish in the top two, they would avoid a home semi‑final at the Royal Exchange, which is currently undergoing refurbishment and could influence the fixture’s impact.

Newcastle, meanwhile, remain shy of securing an A‑list signing, but the potential arrival of Aaron Wainwright could change that narrative for the club’s summer recruitment at Welford Road. Wainwright’s experience and skill set would fill a key gap in Newcastle’s backline, offering the club a tangible upgrade ahead of the upcoming campaign. His signing would also signal a broader ambition to strengthen the squad’s competitiveness in the Premiership. Both clubs, therefore, are positioned to make significant moves as they prepare for a season that promises high stakes and intense competition.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Columbus Crew Fires Reserve Coach Over Sexist Comment to Referee
content:
The Columbus Crew announced the dismissal of reserve‑team coach Alex Morales on Friday after an incident involving a female referee during a match in the MLS Next Pro league. Morales reportedly refused to release his grip on the referee’s hand and subsequently made a remark that the game was “a man’s game,” statements that the club deemed unacceptable.

Club officials stated that the remarks violated the Crew’s code of conduct and the league’s commitment to respect and equality. The incident, which was captured on video and circulated on social media, prompted an internal investigation. Following the review, the Crew confirmed that Morales would no longer hold any coaching responsibilities within the organization.

The Crew’s decision underscores the league’s stance on gender equity and professional conduct. The club has pledged to continue fostering an inclusive environment and will work with MLS to reinforce standards for all staff and players.
author: BBC Sport

title: Premier League early-season points vs xG highlights over‑ and under‑performers
content:
Premier League analysts reviewing the 2025‑26 campaign have identified a clear split between clubs that are converting more points than their expected‑goals (xG) metrics would predict and those falling short of the statistical benchmark. Over‑performers include Newcastle United, whose aggressive pressing has yielded a points‑per‑game rate roughly 0.4 higher than its cumulative xG, and Brighton & Hove Albion, whose efficient finishing and disciplined defensive shape have translated into a surplus of six points relative to their xG tally. Southampton and Brentford also feature among the over‑performers, each posting a modest but notable gap between actual points and the forecasted output derived from shot quality and volume.

Conversely, several high‑profile sides are under‑delivering on the basis of their xG figures. Tottenham Hotspur, despite generating one of the league’s highest xG totals, sit several points below the expected mark, reflecting a persistent inability to capitalize on created chances. Arsenal and Manchester United exhibit similar patterns, with both clubs accruing roughly three to four points fewer than their xG would suggest, indicating inefficiencies in attack and occasional defensive lapses. The disparity between actual results and xG expectations underscores the influence of finishing proficiency, tactical adjustments, and variance on the league table, and it will likely shape transfer and coaching strategies as the season approaches its climax.
author: BBC Sport

title: Lewis Koumas to carry Liverpool form into Wales Nations League
content:
Lewis Koumas has already begun to make an impact in the early stages of the current season, establishing himself as a key player for Liverpool’s midfield. His performances have been marked by a blend of defensive solidity and creative passing, earning praise from the coaching staff and fans alike. The young midfielder’s consistency has helped Liverpool secure a solid start to the campaign, and his contributions have been noted as a bright spot in a squad still finding its rhythm.

Looking ahead, Koumas is set to carry that form into international duty as Wales prepare to face their next Nations League opponent. The Welsh manager has highlighted his recent displays as a factor in the team’s tactical plans, hoping that his composure under pressure and ability to link play will prove valuable against a strong opposition. With the Nations League fixtures carrying significant weight for qualification prospects, both club and country will be keen to see Koumas maintain his high level of performance.

As the season progresses, Lewis Koumas’s dual responsibilities at club and international level underscore his growing importance in modern football. His ability to balance the demands of Premier League competition with the rigors of international duty will be closely watched by supporters and analysts alike, as he seeks to cement his reputation as one of the most promising midfield talents in the game.
author: BBC Sport

title: Klopp Prepares for Germany Debut, Aims to Revive Team's Form
content:
Jurgen Klopp will take charge of the German national team for the first time in a friendly against the United States on Sunday, a match that will serve as a litmus test for the new manager’s approach to a side that has struggled for consistency since the 2018 World Cup. The appointment follows the dismissal of Joachim Löw, who oversaw a disappointing Euro 2024 campaign. Klopp, who has guided Liverpool to Premier League and Champions League glory, arrives with a reputation for high‑intensity football and a focus on squad cohesion, and he is expected to bring a fresh tactical perspective to a team that has yet to find a stable rhythm on the international stage.

BBC Sport notes that Klopp’s strategy will hinge on integrating a mix of experienced players and emerging talents, while instilling a disciplined defensive structure and a rapid transition to attack. He will also need to navigate the expectations of a football‑savvy German fan base and the scrutiny of a media landscape that has been critical of the national side’s recent performances. The friendly against the United States will offer an early gauge of how quickly Klopp can implement his system and whether his experience at club level translates into immediate improvements for Germany’s fortunes on the international scene.
author: BBC Sport

title: Robbie Ure leaves Rangers for Sevilla, Scotland cap on horizon
content:
Robbie Ure has progressed from a stalled spell at Rangers to a key role in Sevilla’s attacking lineup, setting the stage for his first cap for Scotland. After limited opportunities in the Scottish Premiership, the forward moved to Spain where he has consistently contributed goals and assists, helping Sevilla secure a place in the Champions League and cementing his reputation as a reliable striker.

The Scottish national team’s coaching staff have taken note of Ure’s development, and he is now on the cusp of international debut. His performances in La Liga and European competition have demonstrated the pace, composure, and finishing ability that Scotland’s squad requires. If selected, Ure will become the latest product of the Rangers youth system to earn a senior international cap, highlighting the club’s role in nurturing talent that can succeed on the global stage.
author: BBC Sport

title: Raducanu Draws on Agassi's 2009 Autobiography for Comeback
content:
Emma Raducanu has announced a new phase in her comeback, outlining a structured plan to regain her position among the world’s elite tennis players. The former Wimbledon champion, who has struggled with injuries and a dip in form since her 2021 breakthrough, said she is now focused on rebuilding fitness, refining her baseline game, and targeting key tournaments to climb the rankings. Her schedule will include a mix of hard‑court events in the United States and clay‑court tournaments in Europe, with the goal of returning to Grand Slam contention by the next season.

In crafting her strategy, Raducanu cited Andre Agassi’s 2009 memoir, *Open*, as a source of inspiration. Agassi’s candid account of his own battles with self‑doubt, injury, and the pressures of the sport resonated with the Briton, who described the book as a reminder that resilience and honest self‑assessment are essential for long‑term success. By studying Agassi’s approach to mental toughness and his willingness to confront setbacks publicly, Raducanu aims to adopt a similar mindset, focusing on incremental improvement rather than immediate results.

Looking ahead, Raducanu remains determined to re‑establish herself at the top of the game. She plans to use the coming months to solidify her physical conditioning, work closely with her coaching team on tactical adjustments, and gradually re‑enter the competitive circuit. If the outlined plan proves effective, the former Wimbledon champion could reappear on the world stage, bringing her experience and renewed confidence to the sport she has captivated fans worldwide.
author: BBC Sport

title: Live Scouting and Data Cover Most Global Football Talent
content:
Top football clubs are now able to monitor a vast majority of the world’s emerging talent thanks to a combination of live scouting and sophisticated data analytics. By streaming matches in real‑time and collecting detailed performance metrics, clubs can assess players’ technical, tactical, and physical attributes from anywhere on the globe. Advanced video‑analysis software further breaks down individual actions, allowing scouts to spot nuances that were previously missed in traditional scouting reports.

The integration of these tools has expanded the reach of elite academies and transfer departments. Clubs no longer rely solely on regional scouts; instead, they deploy a network of data scientists and analysts who sift through millions of hours of footage to identify promising prospects. This data‑driven approach also facilitates more objective comparisons across leagues and positions, reducing the risk of costly signings and enabling clubs to target niche talent that fits their tactical philosophy.

As a result, the talent pipeline has become more transparent and competitive. Smaller clubs can showcase their players on a global platform, while larger clubs can make informed decisions faster and with greater confidence. The shift toward live scouting and data‑rich analysis is reshaping how football talent is discovered, evaluated, and acquired on an international scale.
author: BBC Sport

title: Cruz Criticizes GOP's 'Right-Wing Socialism' Strategy
content:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R‑TX) criticized a faction of Republicans on Tuesday for advocating what he called “right‑wing socialism,” arguing that the approach would not benefit the party. Speaking on Fox News’s “The Will Cain Show,” Cruz warned that the strategy could alienate voters and weaken the GOP’s electoral prospects. He maintained that the party’s future success depends on appealing to its core supporters rather than adopting policies he deemed too radical.

Cruz identified himself as a populist, noting that his electoral base has consistently comprised blue‑collar workers. He contrasted this demographic with the populist Republicans who push for expansive social programs, labeling their proposals as impractical and potentially damaging to the party’s fiscal credibility. The senator suggested that the GOP should focus on limited government and market‑based solutions that resonate with its traditional constituency.

The remarks come amid growing debate within the party over the direction of its platform and the balance between populist rhetoric and pragmatic governance. Cruz’s comments underscore a broader tension between factions that favor more expansive social policies and those that advocate for a restrained, business‑friendly agenda.
author: The Hill

title: Wicker Criticizes Xi Ahead of Trump Summit
content:
U.S. Senator Roger Wicker of Mississippi criticized Chinese President Xi Jinping on the Senate floor on Tuesday, ahead of the planned summit between President Donald Trump and Xi in Washington, D.C.  Wicker said that if the White House had asked for his input, he would have advised President Trump against inviting Xi to Washington for the meeting.  The senator’s remarks came as the administration prepares to host the two leaders in a high‑profile diplomatic event that could shape U.S.–China relations.

Wicker’s comments underscore the growing skepticism among some Republicans about engaging with Xi, who has been accused of aggressive policies in the South China Sea, human rights abuses in Xinjiang, and a tightening grip on domestic dissent.  The summit, scheduled for the end of the month, is expected to address trade, security, and pandemic cooperation.  While the White House has not yet confirmed the agenda, it has reiterated its commitment to a constructive dialogue with China.

The senator’s statement highlights the broader debate within U.S. politics about the balance between engagement and pressure in dealing with China.  As the summit approaches, lawmakers and officials are likely to weigh the potential benefits of direct talks against concerns over Xi’s leadership style and policy objectives.
author: The Hill

title: UK to review Chagos Islands deal after Trump criticism
content:
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting announced that a formal review of a recent defence procurement agreement would be undertaken, following remarks by U.S. President Joe Biden that the deal was “terrible.” The comments were relayed to Andy Burnham, the UK Labour Party leader, during a briefing on the UK’s latest military purchase. Streeting confirmed that the government would examine the contract’s terms, cost structure and strategic implications to determine whether any adjustments or renegotiations are warranted.

The review will focus on the specific elements that drew criticism, including pricing, delivery schedules and technology transfer provisions. Defence officials say the inquiry will involve consultations with the Ministry of Defence, the Department for International Trade and relevant contractors. The outcome is expected to inform future procurement policy and ensure that UK defence spending aligns with national security priorities and fiscal responsibility.

Streeting said the review would be completed within the next 12 weeks and that the findings would be reported to Parliament. The government has indicated that it remains committed to maintaining strong defence ties with the United States while safeguarding UK interests and ensuring value for money in future acquisitions.
author: BBC Politics

title: UK to fight Russian disinformation and set global AI standards
content:
At a speech to world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly, the United Kingdom’s prime minister said the country could serve as “an honest broker” on artificial intelligence and other pressing global challenges. Speaking in New York, the prime minister called for a coordinated, rules‑based approach to AI governance, arguing that the UK’s experience in technology regulation and its commitment to democratic values position it well to mediate between nations with divergent interests.

The prime minister highlighted the urgency of establishing international norms for AI, citing concerns over security, privacy, and economic disruption. He urged member states to collaborate on safeguards that balance innovation with public safety, and suggested that the UK could host a multilateral forum to draft binding guidelines. Beyond AI, the speech touched on climate change, cybersecurity, and supply‑chain resilience, framing these issues as interconnected and requiring collective action.

In closing, the prime minister reaffirmed the UK’s willingness to take a constructive, facilitative role on the world stage. He emphasized that an “honest broker” would help build trust among nations, ensuring that emerging technologies and global risks are addressed through shared responsibility and transparent dialogue.
author: BBC Politics

title: Taylor to Repeal Climate Policies Within 30 Days
content:
Prime Minister‑elect Angus Taylor has pledged to roll back a range of emissions‑reduction and renewable‑energy policies that were introduced or supported by previous Coalition governments. Within 30 days of a federal election win, his energy spokesperson, Dan Tehan, announced a new bill that would aim to secure “affordable, reliable and secure” energy for Australians. The proposed legislation would scrap vehicle emissions standards, remove the legislated net‑zero‑by‑2050 target, and revoke four of six offshore wind energy zones slated for completion by the late 2030s – the Hunter, Illawarra, Southern Ocean and Bunbury zones. It would also introduce a renewable‑energy code of conduct for developers, mandate that state and territory energy funding prioritise affordability and reliability, and shift the Australian Energy Regulator’s primary focus to those same metrics.

The move has drawn criticism from Liberal and National MPs who argue that the reforms would “let climate change rip” by undermining the country’s climate commitments. Opponents contend that the removal of vehicle emissions standards and the net‑zero target would reverse progress made under previous administrations, while the revocation of offshore wind projects could delay the expansion of renewable capacity. Supporters claim the changes are necessary to curb rising energy costs and protect consumers. The bill will be introduced to parliament in the coming weeks, and its passage will be closely watched by both climate advocates and industry stakeholders.
author: Guardian Environment

title: FDA Delays Approval of Tavneos for Rare Autoimmune Diseases
content:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recently reviewed the approval of Tavneos, a biologic intended to treat a group of rare autoimmune diseases. According to internal FDA records, the agency’s expert panel expressed strong reservations about granting approval. The experts cited concerns that the drug’s safety profile and clinical benefit did not sufficiently outweigh the potential risks for patients with these conditions.

Tavneos is marketed as a therapy for disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus and other autoimmune diseases that affect a small patient population. During the review, the panel examined data from clinical trials, post‑marketing studies, and pharmacovigilance reports. Their critique focused on limited evidence of long‑term efficacy, possible adverse reactions, and the need for more robust comparative data against existing treatments. These points were documented as key factors that could make approval a mistake, according to the agency’s internal deliberations.

The FDA’s review process is designed to balance therapeutic promise with patient safety, and the panel’s concerns underscore the rigorous scrutiny applied to new drugs for rare diseases. While the records reveal the experts’ caution, the final decision on Tavneos’ approval remains unreported in the available documents.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Curtin University launches resource to support brain health and lower dementia risk in Western Australia
content:
Western Australia is expected to experience the fastest rise in dementia cases among Australian states, according to national health projections that highlight an accelerating ageing population and increasing prevalence of risk factors. In response, a new brain‑health resource developed under the leadership of Curtin University has been launched to provide evidence‑based guidance aimed at helping individuals protect cognitive function and lower their likelihood of developing dementia.

The Curtin‑led initiative offers a suite of tools, including an online self‑assessment, educational modules on lifestyle modifications, and resources for caregivers, all aligned with recommendations from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare and the National Health and Medical Research Council. Funded through a partnership of government health agencies and research grants, the program targets Western Australians of all ages, emphasizing early intervention through diet, physical activity, social engagement, and management of chronic conditions. By disseminating practical strategies and up‑to‑date scientific information, the resource seeks to mitigate the projected surge in dementia cases and support community‑wide brain‑health awareness.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Review finds no causal link between prenatal acetaminophen and neurodevelopmental disorders
content:
A comprehensive “umbrella” review published in *Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology* has concluded that existing scientific evidence does not substantiate a causal link between prenatal exposure to the pain reliever paracetamol (acetaminophen) and neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and attention‑deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The analysis pooled data from multiple prior investigations, many of which were limited by small sample sizes, methodological shortcomings, or reported only modest associations between maternal paracetamol use and later child outcomes.

The review highlighted that while earlier studies have suggested possible connections, the overall body of research lacks the robustness required to infer causality.
